PNW Mobile Homes — platform architecture

Date: 29 September 2026 (third revision: Rails, and version 1.0 this week)
Status: Proposed architecture for the whole platform, from the first release in Washington, Oregon and Idaho to national operation. Nothing is implemented yet.
Planning authority: The project room and Ben’s recorded decisions. This document covers the technical design. A proposal here is not a client approval, and the commercial scope of month one stays as agreed in the room until Ben and Moritz change it.

1. The short version

What we are building. The system of record for the manufactured-home market, starting in three states. It covers every home for sale, every model and every dealer who offers it, every place a home can go, every business needed to get it there, and an honest total price. Ben’s own words set the bar: “Build PNW Mobile Homes today as the first region of the company we may want ten years from now.” The buyer he describes should eventually get answers to “Show me 3+ bedroom, 2-bath homes under $180,000 within 200 miles of my ZIP” and to “Can I actually buy this home, put it where I want it, and what will the entire project cost?” This plan designs for both questions now. The first release answers the first, and the second becomes answerable one county at a time.

How it is built. One Ruby on Rails 8 application: server-rendered pages with Hotwire, PostgreSQL with PostGIS on the same small server, Solid Queue for background work in that same database, and Active Storage keeping photos and evidence on Cloudflare R2. Kamal deploys it behind Cloudflare, which also provides DNS, caching, email routing, and Browser Rendering for the dealer websites that need it. Schema-constrained AI extraction feeds the supply engine. Stripe handles billing. Measurement has two layers: PostHog for product analytics, and our own counts for the audience figures that get sold. Version 1.0, the slice that lets Ben sign dealers up, goes live this week on this same foundation (§17).

Five choices that shape the build:

  1. Aggregate first. Every home a participating dealer already advertises gets onto the site from that dealer’s own website, at a permission tier the dealer chose. Dealers then upgrade to managing the listing themselves. This is the room’s “mirror every home in the three states”, which Ben picked to come first, and it is how Kayak works.
  2. The domain model covers the whole vision today. It includes manufacturer plants and options, the identity of a physical home through its HUD labels and serial number, organizations with several roles each, parks and destination sites, sourced rules, a single cost vocabulary, buyer projects, leads and billing. Tables are created as features land. Their keys and relationships are decided now, so nothing built later forces a rewrite of what exists.
  3. AI sits inside the supply pipeline from the first day, behind an evaluation set, typed outputs and approval rules. Hand-written parsers for 65 differently built dealer websites are what does not scale, and Ben’s vision says so: “cannot depend on Ben or staff manually maintaining thousands of listings.”
  4. Revenue and audience evidence are designed in, including enquiries through a relay, seller performance reports, entitlements, placements and billable counters. They are how $1,000 and then $5,000 a month get earned, and they are cheap to build now and expensive to retrofit.
  5. The roadmap runs to national operation. Phases are gated on business outcomes that decide where effort goes next, not on permission to write code. Code is cheap. Data coverage, dealer permission and trust take calendar time, so those start on day one.

2. What the platform is at full scale

Every capability below answers a question Ben has written down. The phase column refers to §17.

The questionCapabilityData it depends onPhase
“What is for sale near me?”Find: one search across every participating dealer, private seller and parkOffers in every tier, geography, freshness1
“Who sells this model, and for how much once delivered?”Compare: model pages that list every offer against a model, in a row-by-row comparisonCatalogue, offer terms, cost vocabulary, transport rates2
“Can I put it where I want it?”Place: park, county and site feasibilityPark policies, jurisdiction rules, HUD zones, sites2–4
“What will the entire project cost?”Total cost: a sourced range covering every componentRate cards, quotes, permits, taxes, park fees3–4
“Who will move it, set it up and insure it, and can I get financing?”Complete: the services network, with introductions the buyer consents toProviders, service areas, licences, consent2–4
“What is my home worth, and how do I sell it?”Sell: the private-seller flow and valuationMarket history across all tiers, outcomes1 / 4
“Can I buy it here?”Transact: deposits and document workflows through licensed partnersDeals, parties, partner integrations5

Businesses get what they will pay for. Dealers get one place to keep inventory, leads they can see arriving, and demand data. Parks fill vacancies. Transporters, installers and contractors get quote requests. Manufacturers get model pages and routing to their retailers. Advertisers get an audience that is measured rather than claimed.

Underneath all of it is a business that runs without Ben. Owners maintain their own records, sources stay in sync by themselves, and any remaining human work lands in short queues that one operator can clear from written playbooks. There is no assistant in the plan, so automation has to keep those queues small.

3. Commitments that are expensive to reverse

Everything else in this document can change cheaply. These ten choices cannot, so they are made now.

  1. Model, physical home and offer are separate records, and a model exists once. Two dealers offering one model are not duplicates. A used home built to that design is a third thing. This comes from Ben: “I don’t want us to build every dealer listing as an isolated item.”
  2. A physical home has an identity. Every transportable section of a HUD-code home carries a certification label, and the home has a manufacturer serial number. When those are known, they are the home’s private key. They let us deduplicate one home across several sources and follow the same home through resales for years, which becomes the provenance record nobody in this market has. They are never shown publicly.
  3. Presence tiers with recorded permission. Every public offer is indexed, mirrored or managed, and no offer is shown at a higher tier than the recorded permission for its source allows. The platform never appears as the seller.
  4. Every fact carries its provenance: its source, when it was observed, who verified it and when it expires. An AI judgment is stored as a judgment. It becomes a fact only through a rule or a person.
  5. Market history is append-only from the first crawl. Asking prices, availability, first-seen and last-seen dates, and outcomes are recorded as observations across all tiers. Valuation, market reports and the “proprietary database” in Ben’s ten-year goal depend on history that cannot be backfilled later.
  6. One cost vocabulary is shared by dealer offer inclusions, provider rate cards, quotes and buyer estimates. Without it, comparison and total cost measure different things.
  7. Organizations have roles. One business record can be a dealer, a transporter and an installer, with memberships, locations, service areas and licences. Separate account types per trade would have to be merged later.
  8. Region and brand are data, and URLs are national from the start. Brands are resolved from the hostname, and each public resource has exactly one canonical host. Changing URL paths later costs search rankings.
  9. The numbers that get billed come from our own records. Impressions, click-outs, enquiries and leads are written to our own store. PostHog analyses them but is never the ledger.
  10. The business owns its assets. Ben’s entity holds the domain, the data, the provider accounts and a copy of the repository it can take away, with portable exports. Infrastructure may start in Moritz’s accounts, but only with a written handover path.

Kept cheap to change on purpose: screens and visual design, search ranking, source adapters, the AI provider and model, prices and plans, email and SMS vendors, and which county is researched next.

Modules

Each module is a namespace that owns its tables and exposes services. Controllers validate input, establish the actor and call services. Imports, operators and sellers all go through the same services, so there is one set of rules for publishing and ownership.

ModuleOwns
Identity & organizationsUsers, sessions, organizations, roles, memberships, licences, verification

HomesPhysical homes, sections, data-plate facts, title status, condition, siting, identity keys

There is no separate HTTP API service for the website. A public partner API (feeds for dealers, syndication) arrives in phase 4 as another entry point over the same services.

Why this stack, briefly

  • Rails rather than Astro on Workers: most of this product is accounts, forms, review screens, background jobs, uploads and email, and Rails 8 ships all of them as one system. Jobs living in the same database remove the plumbing the previous revision needed (outbox, dispatcher, Queues, Workflows, Hyperdrive). The price is one server to run and patch, at about $5–10 a month; Cloudflare stays in front for everything it is good at.
  • Postgres and PostGIS rather than SQLite or D1: polygon service areas, radius search, relational constraints and familiar transactions. The dataset stays well within Postgres at national scale; on the order of 100,000 active offers and tens of millions of observations still fits one well-indexed database with time-partitioned history. PostGIS is used through plain SQL in a few query scopes, so no adapter gem is on the critical path.
  • A purpose-built operator console rather than a CMS: the operator work is claims, match decisions, source failures, rule research and moderation, and no generic admin panel models any of it. Rails makes these screens cheap to build, and under Ben’s “runs without the founder” goal they are the product.
  • Source runs as Solid Queue jobs: a run fetches, renders, snapshots, extracts, matches and applies, backs off politely, and must never overlap a newer run for the same source. Persisted steps plus a per-source concurrency limit give exactly that.
  • No search cluster: measure query plans first. A derived index (ParadeDB or Meilisearch) is a projection that can be rebuilt, and it is added only if relevance or load demands it.

5.10 Invariants the database and domain enforce

Carried from the first draft:

  • Opaque UUIDs identify records. Slugs are presentation only, and a rename creates a redirect.
  • Each mirrored or managed offer has exactly one accountable owner. The marketplace operator is never automatically the seller.
  • A check constraint requires offer_kind to have exactly one matching subject. Dealer versus private and new versus used are separate dimensions.
  • A home’s actual specifications override catalogue defaults. A catalogue edit never silently changes an approved home.
  • Publishing requires an approved revision, verified seller access, a usable contact route, authorized media and a clear moderation status.
  • Every privileged mutation checks membership on the server. Catalogue identity, source permission and live content changes are audited.
  • (source_id, external_item_id) is unique, and content hashes skip unchanged inputs.
  • Optimistic version checks protect seller edits against concurrent imports. There is no last-write-wins.
  • Money is integer cents plus a currency. An unknown price is null, never zero. Units are explicit, and bathrooms may be fractional.
  • Timestamps are stored in UTC. User-facing times carry explicit IANA time zones.

New:

  • An offer’s presence tier never exceeds its source’s current authorization. Revoking permission demotes or removes the offer in the same transaction.
  • An indexed offer always shows its source and links to it. It never uses the source’s photos or prose, and never presents the platform or Ben’s dealership as the seller.
  • Observations and outcomes are insert-only. Corrections are new rows that point at what they correct.
  • A rule with no source, or past its expires_at, cannot produce blocked. It can only produce unknown.
  • A judgment is stored separately from facts and changes state only through a rule, a threshold policy recorded in code, or a person.
  • HUD label numbers, serial numbers, title records, precise private addresses and reported sale prices never reach a public projection, analytics or logs.
  • Regions are not tenants for sellers. Operator permissions may be scoped to regions.

5.11 Model identity and comparison

A canonical model family has explicit variants and revisions. Identical names do not prove identical floorplans or model years. Raw labels are kept on imports and homes, and an uncertain match never blocks a real used home from being listed.

Comparison groups have three levels. Same variant: confirmed identity and year range, so the offers are directly comparable. Same model, different revision: shown together with the differences labelled. Similar class: the same sections, bedroom and bathroom counts and area band, across manufacturers, and never presented as the same home. A factory-order offer needs a seller-confirmed variant, which may be provisional. It is excluded from same-variant comparison until staff verify the variant.

5.12 Geography and privacy

Postal address, physical point, service territory, region membership and brand presentation are separate fields. Country, state and county come from identifier tables, never from hard-coded enums. A private seller chooses how precisely the location is disclosed. Radius search uses the disclosed precision, labels distances as approximate, and is protected against repeated queries that could triangulate a hidden address.

6. The supply engine

6.1 Presence tiers

This design reconciles two things Ben wants: “mirror every home in the three states” and “I do not want to be responsible for creating somebody else’s listing.”

TierWhat a buyer seesPermission requiredWho stands behind itContact routeUpgrade path
IndexedStructured facts (price, beds, baths, size, year, location, dealer), our catalogue match, cost and feasibility context, and “View at [dealer]”Dealer’s recorded yes, or a public-index policy the attorney has approvedThe dealer’s own advertisement; we only point to itTracked click-out to the sourceDealer grants mirroring or claims the listing
MirroredFull listing with the dealer’s photos, a description generated from verified facts, and a freshness stampA recorded yes that covers media and generated textThe dealer, under a standing authorization with correction and removal rightsThe dealer’s chosen route or the relayDealer claims and manages
ManagedFull listing edited and approved by its ownerAn account holder with verified membershipThe owner, revision by revisionRelay and enquiriesPaid placements and pro features

Nothing is published as someone’s listing without them. An indexed entry is a pointer to an advertisement the dealer already runs. Indexed cards carry no photos, which gives every dealer a visible reason to say yes to mirroring. Ben’s dealer calls ask for the easy yes: “Can we show your inventory and send buyers to you?” That is a far smaller ask than “list with us”. The call note becomes the authorization evidence.

Third-party marketplaces (MHVillage, Facebook, Craigslist) are never crawled. A seller may paste text or upload photos from their own advertisement there. We do not fetch those platforms automatically.

6.2 Doorways

Every doorway leads to the same change-set pipeline:

  • Dealer website: a vendor adapter or the generic extractor; one-off, then scheduled.
  • Feed: CSV, XML or a shared spreadsheet, with column mapping learned once per source.
  • File: a spreadsheet, PDF flyer or folder of photos.
  • Forwarded email: sent to a per-organization intake address and parsed by Action Mailbox.
  • Manual entry: the seller workspace, with an editor that shows the listing as it will appear.
  • Private seller on a phone: a camera-first draft that needs no account until publication.
  • SMS or WhatsApp: phase 3, through the same draft model.

6.3 Surveying dealer websites and building adapters

In the first week, before any adapter exists:

  1. Assemble the dealer list: Ben’s 65 locations, cross-checked against the state dealer-licence lookups (§9) and the retailer locators that Clayton, Champion and Cavco publish. Both sources also surface dealers Ben does not know, and the locators show which manufacturers each dealer is authorized to sell.
  2. Fetch each site politely. Fingerprint the platform from generator tags, script hosts, URL patterns, sitemaps, JSON-LD and the JSON endpoints its own inventory widget calls. Group dealers by vendor. Ben already suspects that “some appear to use inventory/catalog systems supplied by manufacturers or industry website providers.”
  3. Build one adapter per vendor template, which then covers every dealer on that vendor. Prefer structured sources in this order: the site’s own feed or API, then JSON-LD and embedded JSON, then HTML.
  4. Send the long tail to the generic AI extractor (§6.5). Use Browser Rendering only where content exists only after JavaScript runs.
  5. Record every site’s robots rules and terms, and store a label for the platform each dealer site runs on. The survey is also the first sales map of the market.

6.4 Pipeline

  Change --> Live[Indexed, mirrored or managed]
  Claim --> Live

A source run is a chain of Solid Queue jobs, limited to one concurrent run per source, with these steps:

  1. Fence: take the source’s fencing token so an older run can never overwrite a newer one.
  2. Fetch and render: within rate limits and robots rules. Snapshots go to R2 under content hashes.
  3. Segment: listing pages into items, spreadsheets into rows, photo folders into proposed homes.
  4. Extract: typed candidates with evidence spans.
  5. Normalize: units, prices and addresses into points and jurisdictions, in code.
  6. Match: to catalogue variants and existing physical homes (§6.6).
  7. Diff: build a change set against current offers.
  8. Apply by tier:
    • Indexed and mirrored changes apply automatically inside the source’s authorization, subject to anomaly guards such as a sudden fall in item count or a price that changes by more than a set threshold.
    • Managed changes become draft revisions that wait for the owner.
  9. Record: write an observation for every item seen.
  10. Project: update the search projection and enqueue follow-up jobs in the same transaction.

Every step records its status, idempotency key, input bounds and versions. Job arguments carry IDs, never documents or credentials. A job can run twice after a crash, so every step is idempotent.

6.5 AI extraction, measured before trusted

Division of labour (unchanged from jev-greenfield.md):

  • Code enumerates candidates wherever structure exists and owns units, arithmetic, validation, state and authorization.
  • A language model returns schema-constrained output for semi-structured pages. It returns values that are already present in the input, together with the spans they came from.
  • Jev answers typed questions with probabilities: which candidate is the year, whether two records are the same home, what a photo shows, whether a condition claim matches the photos.
  • Generative text is written only from verified facts, for descriptions and alt text, and is never a source of facts.

An evaluation set comes before any threshold. From the survey, label at least 60 pages across vendors and the long tail, covering listing recall, per-field accuracy, false merges and cost per item. The extraction model is chosen by that evaluation. Every extraction records its model and prompt version, and a model upgrade has to beat the recorded baseline before it ships.

Thresholds by consequence. Price, beds, baths, year and location need high confidence or a person’s confirmation before an indexed or mirrored offer shows them. Low-confidence fields display as unknown rather than guesses. Managed offers always pass through the owner.

Safety. Source text is untrusted data. It has no tools, cannot change the pipeline and cannot reach secrets, and output must validate against the schema or the item goes to review. If the model is unavailable, adapters and manual review keep working.

Scale economics. Content hashing means unchanged pages are never extracted again. The per-vendor adapters take over the high-volume sources, so AI cost tracks changed long-tail pages, not inventory size (§18).

6.6 Identity resolution and deduplication

  • Exact matches: a known serial or HUD label matches an existing home, subject to a manufacturer and date sanity check.
  • Candidate blocking otherwise: the same seller, or a location within a set distance, plus year, section count, dimensions and price band.
  • Evidence for a match: perceptual hashes of photos (which also catch stolen photos across unrelated sellers, §15), text similarity and a Jev same-home judgment.
  • Outcome: merges are recorded, reversible decisions. Two sources describing one home produce one physical_home with several offers, and the offers are reconciled by tier and ownership. Two dealers offering one model never merge.

6.7 Acquiring the catalogue

Comparison is only as good as the catalogue, and the first draft never said where the catalogue would come from.

  • Seed: harvest model facts from manufacturer websites: names, codes, sections, dimensions, beds, baths, square feet, plants and brand lines. Facts are not copyrightable. Floorplan images and renders are used only with permission.
  • Start with three manufacturers. Clayton (46.4%), Champion (22.8%) and Cavco (17.2%) shipped more than 86% of HUD-code homes in the first quarter of 2026 (MHI market-share report), and all three publish floorplan catalogues. Regional builders follow in order of how often they appear in dealer inventory.
  • Dealer aliases: dealer pages supply alias evidence, such as the variant spellings and codes dealers actually use.
  • Manufacturer partnerships (phase 4): manufacturers want their models shown next to their retailers. A catalogue feed becomes part of a manufacturer programme (§11).
  • Curation: the operator confirms AI-proposed matches in the operator console, a click per model rather than per home, and maintains canonical identities, while dealers propose corrections.
  • Coverage metric: the share of live new-home offers matched to a verified variant, by tier and manufacturer.

6.8 Freshness and sync policy

  • Schedule: daily by default, adjustable per source and per vendor, with per-host concurrency limits.
  • Complete versus partial runs: a run is partial when pagination fails, a login page appears, an item-count anomaly trips or a parse error occurs. Partial runs never remove anything.
  • Indexed offers are pointers: one that is absent from two consecutive complete runs is withdrawn from view, with its observation history kept.
  • Mirrored offers: an absent offer becomes “needs confirmation” and is shown as unconfirmed. After 30 days without confirmation it leaves active search, and it is marked sold only if the source says so.
  • Managed offers: absence never changes them. The owner is nudged at 14 days, shown a warning at 30, and suppressed from active search at 45 unless they confirm.
  • Timestamps: last_seen_at, last_successful_sync_at, last_owner_confirmed_at and price_observed_at stay separate, and the public page shows the right one.

6.9 Conflict policy

Existing stateIncoming source changeBehaviour
Unedited imported draftSame source changedUpdate the draft and keep the evidence
Seller-corrected fieldImport differsKeep the seller’s value and show the conflict
Managed offer, published revisionPrice, specification, identity or location changedCreate a review revision; the approved page stays live
Seller marked sold or withdrawnSource still says availableDo not reactivate; the owner has to act
Fetch or parse failedItems appear to be missingRecord the failure; never infer sold
Authorization revokedWork still pendingStop, demote or remove per the recorded instructions, and purge media

6.10 Claims, outreach and the dealer pipeline

  • Dealer claim: a licence-registry match plus email at the dealer’s own domain, or a callback to the phone number the registry lists. Ben’s personal vouching is one verification route among several, not the only one.
  • Private seller claim: email or phone verification. Drafts prepared by someone else are private and can be deleted in one click, and deletion removes the data.
  • The pipeline is part of the organization record: not_contacted → contacted → permission (index or mirror) → live → claimed → paying, with call notes. It is Ben’s dealer list and the sales pipeline, with no separate CRM to keep in step.
  • Outreach tooling: a record of every contact, one message per person, a do-not-contact list and rate limits enforced in code. These are the rules in distribution.md, made mechanical so they do not depend on willpower.

7. Discovery and comparison

7.1 The search contract

Ben’s acceptance query is a test case: three or more bedrooms, two or more bathrooms, advertised price under $180,000, within 200 miles of a ZIP code.

  1. A validated ZIP resolves to a centroid from a versioned dataset whose rights are documented. ZIP distance is approximate and labelled that way.
  2. The public projection is filtered on publication, moderation, freshness, region, specifications and price.
  3. A GiST index on geography(Point, 4326) serves ST_DWithin, and 200 miles is 321,868.8 m. Physical stock is measured from the home. Factory-order offers are measured from the selling branch and labelled as dealer distance, with delivery estimated separately from the plant.
  4. “From” prices qualify only with the label visible. Quote-only and unknown prices never satisfy a numeric budget. A range qualifies only if its upper bound is within the budget; ranges that straddle the budget appear in a separately labelled section.
  5. Queries are parameterized, sort fields are validated, result sizes are bounded, and pagination is stable.

7.2 Filters

  • Home: price basis, stock, factory order or park space, new or used, beds, baths, year, manufacture before or after the June 1976 HUD code, floor area, sections, manufacturer and model, and roof-load zone (snow country matters in all three states).
  • Location: state, county, city or ZIP, radius, and whether the home must be moved.
  • Park, where the facts are sourced: age restriction, pet types and counts, lot-rent bands (Ben’s: 300 / 400 / 600 / 700 / 800+, doubled around Seattle), and home-age rules.
  • Unknown values never pass a hard filter silently. The buyer can include them explicitly, and they are labelled.

7.3 Results and ranking

Cards show the actual seller, presence tier, price basis, location precision, relocation status and the right freshness date. Ranking is documented: relevance, distance, price or newest, with a completeness-and-freshness factor that is published in plain words. Paid placement appears only in labelled slots, satisfies the buyer’s filters, and never changes the organic order. Empty results offer ways to widen the search, and every zero-result query is recorded as a supply signal.

7.4 Model pages and the comparison

A model page is the Kayak page Ben described:

  • Catalogue facts, floorplan and zones.
  • Every offer against the model, both in-stock units and factory-order offers, from every dealer.
  • One comparison row per dealer: price basis, what is included by cost component, lead time, distance, and an estimated delivered-and-set range to the buyer’s ZIP (§8).
  • Inclusions the dealer has not stated are shown as unknown, never as zero, with a request a quote action that becomes a lead.

Model pages are also the platform’s strongest search asset, because people search for model names.

7.5 Alerts, favourites and comparisons

Saved searches with consented email alerts arrive early, in phase 2. They are the cheapest repeat-traffic engine a marketplace has, and they rebuild the email list on a clean consent basis alongside the old ~4,000 addresses. Favourites and side-by-side comparisons work without an account, and signing in keeps them.

7.6 Search read model

public_offer_search is a projection. For managed offers it is updated inside the publication transaction. For indexed and mirrored offers it is updated inside the source-run apply step. It can be rebuilt from the source tables. Indexes: B-tree for publication, region and price predicates; GiST for geography; GIN for a search vector that combines exact model and alias matching with full-text search.

8. Total cost and feasibility

8.1 Honesty rules

  • Every figure is a range, with its sources and dates on view.
  • Unknown is not zero.
  • Blocked requires a sourced, unexpired rule. Anything short of that is unknown, with the question the buyer should ask.
  • This is information, not advice or a credit decision. It never claims a home will be approved or financed.

Ben’s own framing sets the target: “They see a home advertised for $80,000 and think it costs $80,000.”

8.2 Cost components

Offer inclusions, provider rate cards, quotes and buyer estimates all use one vocabulary.

CodeComponentTypically quoted by

tax_clearanceTaxes due before a move, and move permitsCounty or seller

park_entryApplication fee, deposit, first month’s lot rentPark

8.3 Rules

Rule familyExamplesTypical source
Jurisdiction placementWhether manufactured homes are allowed in the zone; minimum year, width or size; roof pitch or siding; foundation; required snow or roof-load zoneCounty and city codes, planning departments
Park acceptanceHome age, size and style; condition; 55-and-over status; pets; application criteriaPark operators and their documents
TransportWidth and length limits, escort thresholds, oversize permits, taxes due before a moveWSDOT, ODOT and ITD oversize permits; county treasurer tax certificate before a move in WA; county tax collector notice and payment in OR (ORS 308.865); in ID, a reversal of declaration for homes converted to real property

Rules are authored in the operator console, versioned, sourced, and given an expiry that forces re-verification. An evaluation stores the rule versions it used, so an answer given in March can be explained in June.

8.4 The evaluator

Detailed diagram specification
flowchart TD
  Project[Buyer project and destination] --> Eval[Deterministic evaluator]
  Homes[Candidate homes and offers] --> Eval
  Rules[Sourced placement and loan rules] --> Eval
  Rates[Rate cards and quotes] --> Eval
  Jev[Jev: needs and qualitative fit] --> Eval
  Eval --> Verdict[Verdict and cost range]
  Verdict --> Referral[Consented provider referral]
  • Constraints use three values: satisfied, violated or unknown. From those the evaluator returns feasible, feasible if… (naming the condition), blocked by… (naming the rule and its source) or unknown (naming what to ask).
  • Cost: the sum of component ranges. Transport comes from the county-centroid road-distance matrix, refined with the actual route when a quote is requested, times rate-card structures plus adders for sections and escorts. Setup and foundation come from regional rate cards. Taxes and permits come from rules.
  • Jev’s part: it reads a buyer’s free-text situation into typed needs with evidence spans, for example “land outside Yakima, about $60,000, two dogs”. It also judges qualitative fit. It never decides a hard gate.
  • Privacy: sensitive household facts (income or credit bands, ages) can be evaluated without being stored, and never reach analytics.

8.5 Acquiring the rules, led by demand

No one researches 119 counties and hundreds of parks up front. Research is ordered by demand: search destinations, zero-result queries and project destinations rank counties and parks by buyer interest. A research_task queue with written playbooks lets an operator verify rules by document and phone. Park operators who claim their park maintain its policies themselves, under expiry dates. Coverage is published per county (“feasibility available for 14 counties”) so nobody mistakes gaps for answers.

8.6 Valuation

Sellers “struggle to know what their home is actually worth.” Once a year of observations exists, the platform can show comparables drawn from market history across all tiers (year, size, sections, condition, region and time on market), with ranges and the comparables shown. A hedonic model can follow when volume supports one. This is the clearest use of commitment 5.

9. Places and the services network

Parks. Seed park records from the state registries where they exist, then enrich them from the web and by phone:

  • Washington: the Department of Revenue runs the park registration programme (RCW 59.30.050) and keeps a database of about 1,200 registered communities, a figure from a secondary source. A copy is requested through a records request.
  • Oregon: OHCS publishes its manufactured dwelling park directory as a downloadable dataset on data.oregon.gov.
  • Idaho: there is no state registry. Parks are seeded from county records, the web and dealer knowledge, and this is where Ben’s calls matter most.

Each park gets a page with the homes for sale in it, vacant spaces, lot rent and rules. Operators claim the page to keep it accurate and to list vacancies as space_for_rent offers. The park map is a view over these records. Building it is also how the platform meets every park manager in three states, and those managers are a supply source, an audience and future advertisers.

Service providers. Seed dealers and installers from the state licensing lookups:

  • Washington: dealers through the Department of Licensing (RCW 46.70); installers certified by Labor & Industries.
  • Oregon: dealers through the Division of Financial Regulation (ORS 446.691); installers licensed by the Building Codes Division.
  • Idaho: dealers, brokers and installers through DOPL.

Transporters and contractors are seeded from registries and the web. Each gets a free profile with service areas and, where the provider supplies them, rate cards. Buyers can request quotes, and providers see a log of every referral sent to them. That log is what turns a free profile into a paid one in phase 3.

Lenders and insurers. Directory entries describe programme attributes (home age limits, foundation requirements, personal versus real property). Introductions happen only with buyer consent. RESPA Section 8 covers loans secured by real property, including a manufactured home on land. Chattel loans secured by the home alone generally fall outside it. The CFPB’s 2023 advisory opinion on comparison-shopping platforms treats three things together as a kickback: non-neutral presentation, steering, and pay tied to that steering. So lender listings are presented neutrally, and lenders pay flat fees not tied to referral volume until counsel approves anything else (§15).

Land. Sites begin as a point with its jurisdiction. Parcel boundaries and zoning come later, from county GIS layers or a licensed parcel dataset, when demand for private-land placement justifies it.

10. Engagement: click-outs, enquiries and leads

  • By tier: indexed offers send buyers out through a tracked click-out. Mirrored and managed offers take an enquiry form with a masked email relay, and masked phone numbers come later.
  • Why the relay matters:
    • Private sellers stay safe.
    • Relay messages are screened for scam patterns: requests for payment off the platform, “I am overseas, pay a deposit”, gift cards.
    • Enquiries become measurable, and measured enquiries are the thing dealers and providers will pay for.
    • Seller response times become visible.
  • Lifecycle: saved → delivered → replied (a reply seen through the relay) → marked qualified (optional feedback from either side) → outcome.
  • Second needs: an enquiry often implies a move, a place to put the home, setup or insurance. The buyer is offered consented introductions, and each accepted introduction is a lead routed to a provider covering that area. This is jev-greenfield.md idea 5, starting with transport and setup, where the regulations are simple.
  • Seller reports: a weekly digest of views, saves, click-outs and enquiries per listing and per organization. This is the dealer retention loop and the natural moment to offer upgrades.

11. Revenue architecture

StreamWho paysWhat they getBillable unitPhase
Featured placementDealers, private sellersLabelled top slots in search, model and county pagesListing × period3
Dealer pro subscriptionDealersManaged sync, relay and leads, demand insights, enhanced profile, feed exportMonthly3
Provider subscription and leadsTransporters, installers, contractorsProfile placement, quote requests, referral logMonthly, or per accepted lead3
Park programmeParksVacancy promotion, enhanced page, applicant enquiriesMonthly3–4
Sponsorship and advertisingRegional businesses, insurers, lenders (flat)County, category and newsletter placementsFlat monthly or CPM3
Private-seller upgradesPrivate sellersFeatured slot, valuation report, more photosOne-off3–4
Manufacturer programmeManufacturersEnhanced model pages, retailer routing, demand by countyAnnual4
Market insightsDealers, manufacturers, lendersAggregated demand and supply by county, model and priceSubscription4–5
Transaction servicesBuyers or sellers, through a partnerDeposits held in escrow, document workflowsPer transaction5, after licensing review

Mechanics.

  • Stripe products map to plan rows. Plans grant entitlements held in Postgres, never in feature flags, and entitlements unlock placements and features.
  • Checkout, the customer portal and Stripe Tax make buying self-serve, so an advertiser can buy a county sponsorship at 2 a.m. without Ben.
  • Signed webhooks feed an idempotent billing ledger.
  • Advertiser and seller reports read from billable_counter and reconcile with Stripe. PostHog is used for analysis only.

The milestones in numbers (illustrative, not forecasts):

  • $1,000 a month is about ten dealers on a $99 pro plan, or a mix such as five pro dealers, a handful of featured listings and two county sponsors.
  • $5,000 or more a month is roughly 30–50 paying businesses across dealers, providers and parks, plus sponsorship.
  • Multi-million annual revenue is the same product repeated across regions: thousands of paying businesses, lead revenue and data products.

The architecture changes very little between the three. What changes is coverage and audience, which is why the audience layer (§12) matters so much.

Deliberately left out of the table: success fees or commissions on home sales. In Washington, being paid by a seller for finding a buyer falls within the dealer licence, and Idaho licenses brokers. Ben kept the door to commissions open, so treat them as a licensing decision and not a pricing tweak (§15).

12. Measurement

12.1 Two layers

  1. Complete first-party counts. Rails records one count per public page view, click-out, enquiry and placement impression, keyed by page type, region, county, offer and organization. Counts are buffered and rolled up by a scheduled job into daily aggregates in Postgres, kept permanently. No cookies and no personal data are involved, and Cloudflare’s own traffic analytics serve as a cross-check. These counts are the audience number for advertisers and the figures in seller reports, and they replace the stale 3,000-visitor claim with a measured one.
  2. Behavioural analytics in PostHog Cloud (US region, a dedicated PNW production project, and a separate or disabled development project) for funnels, product analytics, error tracking, masked replay, flags and experiments.

Postgres remains authoritative for accounts, offers, approvals, jobs and money. If analytics fails, nothing else does.

12.2 Privacy posture: a correction to the first draft

The first draft proposed opt-in analytics. For a US marketplace whose product is an audience, opt-in would undercount exactly the number being sold, and in these three states it goes beyond what the law requires. The state positions:

  • Washington has no comprehensive consumer privacy law; My Health My Data covers health data only.
  • Idaho has no comprehensive consumer privacy law either (checked against secondary trackers).
  • Oregon’s Consumer Privacy Act applies from 100,000 Oregon consumers a year, or 25,000 consumers where a quarter of revenue comes from selling personal data. First-party analytics that is not sold and not used for cross-context targeted advertising falls under its opt-out regime, and since January 2026 Oregon requires honouring universal opt-out signals.

The proposal instead:

  • Cookieless first-party counts for everyone.
  • PostHog enabled by default, with a clear privacy notice and an easy opt-out.
  • The Global Privacy Control signal honoured as an opt-out from the first day, before any threshold applies.
  • Visitors who opt out or send GPC are still counted, in PostHog’s cookieless mode, which stores nothing on their device.
  • No sale or sharing of personal data, and no third-party advertising pixels without a separate decision.
  • Replay sampled and masked, and never recorded on authentication, claim, draft, upload, enquiry, billing or operator screens.

Counsel reviews the privacy notice before launch.

12.3 Capture rules

These carry over from the first draft:

  • posthog-js is initialized once in the public shell, with pageviews configured explicitly and broad autocapture off at first. Turbo navigation must not double-count.
  • A first-party proxy has fixed upstreams, restricted paths and bounded bodies, and forwards no application cookies or authorization headers.
  • posthog-ruby in background jobs emits server events for committed business facts, enqueued in the same transaction as the fact, with stable event UUIDs for deduplication and the original timestamps. Events that describe the same milestone are never emitted from both browser and server.
  • Identity is an opaque user ID after sign-in and is reset on logout. The active organization is a property. System jobs use operation identities with person processing disabled.
  • Properties are typed, versioned and allowlisted. Contact details, message text, precise buyer locations, sensitive project fields and documents are never sent.
  • Missing configuration is a development error and a no-op in production, and production configuration health is monitored separately.

12.4 Event registry (initial)

EventProducer and trigger
$pageviewBrowser; one real navigation, with a sanitized URL and page type
search:results_viewBrowser; result set rendered, with bounded filters, count, radius band and latency
offer:viewBrowser; detail shown, with tier, kind and price basis
offer:click_outServer; tracked redirect to the source committed
enquiry:submit / enquiry:deliver / enquiry:replyServer; each state committed in the relay
lead:create / lead:acceptServer; consented introduction created or accepted by a provider
alert:subscribe_confirm / alert:sendServer
seller:signup_complete / org:claim_completeServer
listing:draft_create / listing:approve / listing:publish / listing:revision_publishServer; publication milestones, where a first publish happens once per offer
listing:availability_changeServer; previous and new status, and the actor category

12.5 North-star measures and dashboards

  • Buyer value: external enquiries delivered plus click-outs, per week, over distinct offers. Click-outs measure intent and delivered enquiries measure contact, and the two are reported separately.
  • Supply: live offers by tier and kind; coverage, meaning indexed offers as a share of the known regional inventory from the survey; and catalogue match rate.
  • Business: paying organizations, monthly recurring revenue, and leads accepted.
  • Efficiency: operator minutes per live offer and per verified rule, which should fall every month.

Dashboards: Audience; Buyer discovery (search → view → click-out or enquiry); Supply activation (permission → live → claimed → paying); Intake friction; Search gaps; Reliability; Revenue. Reports use Pacific weeks and exclude internal, QA and bot traffic.

13. Regions, brands and national expansion

  • Region: a set of counties with a status, a brand, default content, and operators with region-scoped permissions. Adding a region is configuration plus data, never a code fork.
  • Brand: a set of hostnames, a name, a theme and the regions it serves, resolved per request from the hostname.
  • Canonical host: every public resource has one, namely the brand serving the region the resource sits in. URL paths are the same on every host, so a future national brand is a redirect map and not a rewrite. Decide before the second region whether regional brands stay canonical or a national brand takes over with regional landing pages. The naming of the national company is Ben’s call.
  • The region launch playbook runs as code:
    1. Import the dealer and installer licence lookups, the manufacturers’ retailer locators and any state park registries for the new states. Where a state has no registry, as in Idaho, plan research tasks instead.
    2. Seed jurisdictions.
    3. Run the dealer-site survey.
    4. Assign operators.
    5. Generate county pages from templates that stay unpublished until they pass inventory thresholds.
    6. Score readiness.
  • National scale:
    • Observations are partitioned by month, with a read replica for analytics queries.
    • The crawler scales by vendor adapters and scheduling, not by head count.
    • Operator teams are organized by region.
    • A derived search index is added only if measured load requires it.
  • Languages: interface strings are externalized from the first line of code. Spanish is the likeliest second language for buyers in this region, and it is added when search and enquiry data show demand.

14. Pages, search engines and content

14.1 URL scheme (fixed now)

ResourcePathIndexed by search engines
Inventory search/homes/ with normalized, shareable filtersCanonical base only
Home offer/homes/<public-id>/<slug>/Mirrored and managed: yes. Indexed tier: noindex, because it is a pointer to the dealer’s page
Factory-order offer/offers/<public-id>/<slug>/Yes
Model/models/<manufacturer>/<model>/Yes; the core search asset
Manufacturer/manufacturers/<manufacturer>/Yes
Dealer or business/dealers/<public-id>/<slug>/, /services/<category>/<public-id>/<slug>/Yes when claimed or sufficiently complete
Park/parks/<state>/<slug>/Yes when sourced
Place/<state>/, /<state>/<county>/, /<state>/<county>/<city>/Only above inventory and content thresholds
Guides/guides/<slug>/Yes
Account, operator console, previews/account/, /ops/, /review/<token>Never

Titles and descriptions are unique. The HTML carries real content with ordinary links, alt text written from verified facts, breadcrumbs, Open Graph tags and a sitemap index restricted to published canonical pages, with truthful lastmod values. Structured data matches what each page actually is. A sold offer stays visible with its state and alternatives for a set period and then returns 410, and model pages remain after individual offers sell.

14.2 Content

Guides, regional copy and page blocks live in the database with revisions and approval, edited in Markdown in the operator console. The first draft put MDX in the repository, which would have made every article a developer task. Ben’s decade of experience is the moat: the recorded interviews (Tuesdays) become the guides on what a move really costs, why 1976 matters, reading a park’s rules and selling without a dealer. AI helps with transcription and editing. It does not write the guides.

14.3 Media

  • Upload: scoped, short-lived uploads into private R2. Type, size and decoded pixel limits are validated by content.
  • Originals: EXIF and location data are stripped from public derivatives, and originals are kept as restricted evidence.
  • Hashing: perceptual hashes are computed on ingest (§6.6, §15).
  • Derivatives: bounded sizes with explicit dimensions, a prioritized hero image and lazy loading below the fold.
  • Takedown: withdrawal revokes access at the origin, purges the CDN and leaves a tombstone so a retry cannot republish the file.
  • Open decision: a representative media spike decides between Cloudflare Images transformations and precomputed derivatives.

14.4 Migrating from Brilliant Directories and cutting over

  1. Export what BD actually provides: listings, contacts, images with their rights, URLs, metadata and DNS records. Keep the original export read-only.
  2. Treat old listings as unverified until the owner confirms them. Transfer no accounts or passwords, and invite owners to claim instead.
  3. Inventory the DNS zone (mail, SPF, DKIM, DMARC, verification records, DNSSEC and any third-party subdomains). Copy it and check it before switching nameservers, and coordinate DS records with the registrar if DNSSEC is on.
  4. Build on a protected preview hostname that is not indexed. The DNS move and the website origin switch are separate changes.
  5. Map old URLs to new ones and test apex and www behaviour, HTTPS, mail, search and contact.
  6. Cut over after a data snapshot, freezing legacy writes during the window.
  7. Watch errors, contact routes, indexing and mail. A fallback to BD must account for anything created on the new platform, because BD is not a synchronized backup.

The newsletter list turned out to be 789 addresses, exported from Wix and collected through the old site’s sign-up form under a policy covering newsletters and updates. It is mailed once, from Ben, when the new site has homes on it, from a separate marketing subdomain, with an unsubscribe link and the suppression list honoured.

15. Trust, safety and legal posture

  • Venue, not seller.
    • The terms of service, page copy and attribution say who is selling.
    • Descriptions generated from facts are approved by the owner before they appear on mirrored or managed offers.
    • Third-party content is the seller’s.
    • A copyright agent is registered for notices about photos.
  • Verification levels, shown as badges: email → phone → licence-verified business → optional identity verification for private sellers through a provider. “Every listing on this site is checked” is claimed only once the checks exist and run.
  • Moderation.
    • Automated checks for duplicates, fraud patterns and prohibited content.
    • Fair-housing language screening: advertising that states a preference by familial status is blocked unless the community has claimed the housing-for-older-persons exemption. That exemption requires at least 80% of occupied units to have a resident aged 55 or over, published policies, and age verification. The claim is recorded and shown as the park’s own statement. The advertising rule (42 USC 3604(c)) applies to the notice itself, which is why submitted text is screened rather than trusted.
    • A human queue for everything flagged.
  • Fraud signals:
    • Photo hashes reused by unrelated sellers.
    • Prices far below comparables.
    • Velocity of new accounts.
    • Relay messages asking for payment before a viewing or off the platform.
    • Clear buyer warnings, and a report route on every page.
  • Questions for Ben’s attorney, who is already booked for seller identity:
    1. Indexing dealers who have not answered, meaning the public-index policy in §6.1.
    2. The final seller-identity wording.
    3. Whether any commission on home sales would trigger licensing. Washington’s definition of a “listing dealer” (RCW 46.70.011) covers being paid by a seller for finding a willing buyer, and Idaho licenses manufactured-home brokers separately from dealers. Assume no success fees on home sales unless the business holds the licence; advertising, subscriptions and flat lead fees paid by businesses are the default.
    4. Lender referrals and compensation under RESPA.
    5. The privacy notice and terms of service.
  • Security.
    • Access: ownership is enforced at every read and write boundary, including media, drafts, imports and jobs.
    • Data exposure: public responses are explicit projections. Separate migration and runtime roles.
    • Sessions: secure HttpOnly cookies, origin and CSRF checks, rate limits on login and claim, expiring single-use hashed tokens with a confirmation step (safe against link scanners), and stronger authentication for administrators and ownership changes.
    • Importer network access: authorized HTTPS hosts only. Private, local and link-local addresses, credentials in URLs, unexpected ports, oversized downloads and redirects or DNS rebinding to disallowed targets are all refused. There is no general URL-fetch endpoint.
    • Untrusted content: listing HTML is escaped, rich text sanitized and documents parsed in isolation.
    • Secrets: environment-scoped, and never present in the repository, logs, room answers or analytics.
  • Retention.
    • Proposed defaults: abandoned anonymous drafts 7 days, unclaimed prepared drafts 30 days, raw snapshots 90 days (longer only while a dispute or permission record requires it), operational logs 30 days, and replay 30 days or less.
    • Kept longer: observations and outcomes are kept without personal data for the life of the platform.
    • Deletion and export: these cover application data, media, jobs, marketing preferences and PostHog person data. Tombstones stop imports and delayed events from recreating deleted data, and a restore re-applies deletions before exposure.

16. Operations: a business that runs without Ben

  • The operator console is a set of queues, each with an owner role, a service level and a linked playbook:
    • claims and verification
    • match decisions
    • source failures and anomalies
    • moderation and reports
    • rule and park research
    • relay escalations
    • billing exceptions
  • Automation-first: a person sees only what automation could not settle, and every manual action is logged so it can be automated next.
  • Roles: platform administrator and operator (Moritz at first; no assistant is planned); regional operators later, if expansion needs them. Operator permissions can be scoped to regions.
  • The efficiency target: operator minutes per live offer, reviewed monthly. The business is working when that number falls while coverage rises.
  • Self-service for owners: edit, mark sold, remove, claim, invite colleagues, connect a source, buy, cancel, download invoices.
  • Service targets:
    • Warm search p95 under 500 ms on representative data, with cold starts measured separately.
    • Mobile p75 LCP ≤ 2.5 s, INP ≤ 200 ms and CLS ≤ 0.1, measured on real visits.
    • An owner’s sold action takes effect immediately, followed by a cache purge.
    • No accepted job is ever without a persisted status.
    • RPO ≤ 24 h through an independent daily backup; RTO ≤ 4 h during staffed hours, proven by a rehearsed restore.
    • Alert when the job backlog passes 15 minutes.
  • Failure behaviour:
    • PostHog down: the application continues.
    • A source down or changed: approved content is kept, source health is marked, and nothing is mass-marked sold.
    • Database down: writes fail clearly and never show “saved”.
    • Jobs stalled: the work stays in Postgres and resumes when the worker restarts.
    • Email down: retried, and identity proof is never bypassed.
    • AI down: adapters and manual review continue.
    • Image variants failing: previously made variants or a placeholder, never originals.
  • Alerting: Moritz receives infrastructure alerts. Ben receives a weekly business summary, never a pager. Name a backup operator before promising continuous support.
  • Backups and portability: a nightly encrypted logical backup and media manifest to R2 under separate credentials, plus server snapshots; when Postgres moves to a managed service, its restore window adds to this. R2 lifecycle rules match the recovery needs. Restores are rehearsed before launch and after major schema changes. Exports are standard Postgres plus media keys.
  • Delivery practice:
    • Local Postgres and PostGIS with synthetic fixtures.
    • A staging hostname with isolated data, buckets and secrets, email suppression and production analytics off.
    • CI runs the test suite, RuboCop, Brakeman, migration checks, the extraction evaluation (on adapter or prompt changes) and system tests of the seller and buyer paths. Kamal deploys without downtime.
    • The server runs unattended security updates, and disk, memory and backup freshness are monitored.
    • Additive migrations that work with both the old and new versions; idempotent seeds.

Repository shape

app/
  models/           one namespace per module (§4): catalogue, homes, market, supply, places…
  services/         domain services and rules
  controllers/      public pages, seller workspace, operator console (/ops)
  views/            ERB with Turbo; components where they pay
  jobs/             source runs, extraction, digests, roll-ups, backups
  mailboxes/        enquiry relay and forwarded inventory (Action Mailbox)
config/
  recurring.yml     schedules
  deploy.yml        Kamal
db/                 migrations, PostGIS SQL, seeds
eval/               labelled pages and extraction benchmarks
docs/               architecture and decision records

17. Roadmap

Principles. Code is the fast clock. Dealer permission, catalogue curation, park and county research, the attorney, newsletter consent and trust are the slow clocks, so they start in the first week. Every phase ships to production. Each phase’s signals decide where effort goes next. They are not permission to build.

PhaseWindowThemeExit signals
1.0This weekDealer sign-up and first homesBen can send the sign-up link; the first dealers’ homes live; his test query works; DNS on Cloudflare
1OctoberLive in three statesHundreds of homes live across tiers; Ben’s acceptance query works; measured traffic; BD retired
2Months 2–3Compare and returnModel comparison live with delivered-cost ranges; alerts sending; parks and providers seeded
3Months 3–6EarnPaid products self-serve; $1,000 a month; first leads accepted by providers
4Months 6–24Deepen and replicateFeasibility for high-demand counties; valuation; manufacturer programme; second region; $5,000+ a month
5Years 2–10NationalRegion playbook repeated; national brand; partner API; transaction services

Version 1.0: dealer sign-up and first homes (this week)

The smallest release that lets Ben sign dealers up, on the full plan’s schema and stack, so later phases add to it rather than replace it.

  • Dealer sign-up at pnwmobilehomes.com/join: business, inventory page, contact, the choice of tier, and plain-language terms. Ben can fill it in during a call for a verbal yes. Every sign-up notifies Ben and Moritz, and the form is the permission record (§6.1).
  • Import: fetch the dealer’s inventory page, extract with AI into typed fields, deduplicate, and publish at the chosen tier. Moritz approves each dealer’s first import with one click; after that, a daily re-check runs, and partial runs never remove anything. Observations are recorded from the first run.
  • Listing a home yourself with an emailed sign-in link: add a home with photos, edit it, mark it sold. This covers Ben’s own homes, private sellers and dealers without a website.
  • Search with price, beds, baths, year, size, width, new or used, must-be-moved, and ZIP plus radius, so Ben’s test query passes. Home and dealer pages, and a homepage.
  • Contact: tracked click-outs for linked homes, and an enquiry form that emails the seller for self-listed ones.
  • Measurement from the first week: PostHog, plus our own view and click-out counts per home and dealer.
  • Legal pages: terms, privacy and removal requests, as plain-language drafts for the attorney to review.
  • Not in 1.0: comparison, alerts, parks, providers, payments, feasibility, the masked relay and Spanish, all in later phases.
  • Running cost: one small server (about $5–10 a month). Everything else sits in free allowances, and the one-off AI import is covered by the month-one fee.
  • Already done: the Cloudflare zone with every existing record copied, and Email Routing addresses. The nameserver switch is the last step.

Phase 1: live in three states (October)

What gets built:

  • Tables for the catalogue, homes, organizations, market (all tiers), places (regions, jurisdictions, a minimal park table), provenance, engagement (click-outs, enquiries) and measurement.
  • Vendor adapters plus the generic extractor, daily sync and observations from the first run.
  • Catalogue seeds for the manufacturers dealers carry, with Moritz confirming matches in the operator console.
  • The seller workspace (managed offers, approvals, sold and withdrawn) and the private-seller camera flow.
  • Search with Ben’s acceptance query and filters; offer, dealer, model (without the comparison layer), state and county pages.
  • The enquiry relay; first-party counts and PostHog; the operator console queues for claims, matches, source failures and moderation.
  • Media, SEO foundations, the BD migration and the cutover.

Targets. These depend on Ben’s calls, since supply is his side of the work:

  • At least 25 dealer locations granting index or mirror permission, and 300 or more homes live across tiers.
  • Ben’s own current and past homes live as managed offers.
  • At least one private seller completing the flow unaided.
  • At least 80% of new-home offers matched to a catalogue variant.
  • A real weekly audience number.

Phase 2: compare and return (months 2–3)

  • The comparison layer on model pages, with delivered-and-set ranges from transport rate cards and the county distance matrix.
  • Saved searches and alerts; favourites and comparisons.
  • Newsletter relaunch, if consent checks pass.
  • Park records seeded from registries, with park pages and claims; provider profiles seeded from licence registries, with service areas and quote requests.
  • Weekly seller reports; the claim-to-managed flow and scheduled sync with owner delegation.
  • Spanish-ready strings.

Phase 3: earn (months 3–6)

  • Stripe plans, entitlements and self-serve checkout.
  • Featured placement, the dealer pro plan and provider plans.
  • County and category sponsorships with first-party reports.
  • Park vacancy offers.
  • Second-need detection and consented leads for transport and setup.
  • Feasibility version 1 for the counties that search demand ranks highest.
  • SMS and WhatsApp intake.

Phase 4: deepen and replicate (months 6–24)

  • Feasibility expanded county by county, and buyer projects end to end.
  • Valuation from comparables.
  • The lender and insurer directory, with the compensation model counsel approves.
  • The manufacturer programme and catalogue feeds; market insights for dealers; masked phone numbers.
  • Spanish for buyers, if demand shows.
  • The second region, launched from the playbook, and the decision on a national brand.

Phase 5: national (years 2–10)

  • The region playbook repeated, with regional operators or partners.
  • A partner API and syndication feeds, so dealers list once and publish everywhere.
  • Transaction services through a licensed partner.
  • Data partnerships.
  • A national brand fronting regional pages.

Evidence required before each public launch

  • Same-model offers from two dealers stay separate, and a used home can exist with no known model.
  • Two sources describing one home produce one physical home, a merge can be reversed, and two dealers’ offers of one model never merge.
  • No offer’s tier exceeds its authorization, and revoking an authorization demotes the offer immediately and purges its media.
  • Isolation between sellers holds for offer IDs, imports, claims, media and jobs.
  • Replayed runs and duplicate queue deliveries create neither duplicates nor repeated first-publication events. Seller edits survive changes at the source, an old run cannot overwrite a newer one, and a failed or partial run never means sold.
  • No draft, private address, HUD label, serial, token or document leaks through server rendering, JSON, media, caches, replay, errors or analytics.
  • The acceptance query behaves correctly at its boundaries, including the labels for stock versus factory order and for price uncertainty.
  • Search, contact and enquiries work with analytics blocked and with PostHog unavailable.
  • Backups restore, rollbacks preserve accepted writes, and DNS and mail checks pass.
  • Ben and at least one dealer complete their real workflows without Moritz editing database rows for them.

Notes on the estimates.

  • AI extraction. At current Anthropic list prices (Claude Sonnet 5 at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens; Claude Haiku 4.5 at $1 and $5; the Batch API at half price), extracting a page of about 6,000 input and 1,000 output tokens costs roughly $0.02 on Sonnet 5.
    • Initial extraction: about 800 pages for 65 dealers, or about $20.
    • Daily re-sync: about $0.50–1.00 a day after content hashing, lower with batching.
    • National scale: cost is kept down by vendor adapters, not by head count.
  • Cloudflare list prices checked 28 September:
    • DNS, CDN and Email Routing are free.
    • R2 includes 10 GB a month free, then costs $0.015 per GB-month.
    • Browser Rendering gives 10 minutes a day on the free plan; on Workers Paid ($5 a month), 10 browser-hours a month are included, then $0.09 an hour.
    • Email Service (in beta, Workers Paid) includes 3,000 emails a month, then costs $0.35 per 1,000.
  • The server: a small US VPS; Hetzner’s Hillsboro, Oregon location suits a PNW audience. Confirm the current price when ordering.
  • Neon Launch, for later: $0.106 per CU-hour and $0.35 per GB-month, with always-on compute available.
  • PostHog’s free allowances: 1 million events, 5,000 recordings, 1 million flag requests and 100,000 exceptions a month.
  • Stripe: its fees are a percentage of revenue and sit outside this table.
  • Who pays: running costs are Ben’s, and small at the start. The month-one fee covers AI spend. Infrastructure starts in Moritz’s accounts, registered to ops@pnwmobilehomes.com, so a later handover changes billing and forwarding, not logins.
  • Review: check actual usage weekly during phase 1. Cut replay and speculative enrichment before touching inventory integrity or recovery.
